arguments.title: Alex 2026 self-review — evidence draft
arguments.body:
Scope and framing

This document gathers concrete evidence for my 2026 self-review narrative, organized around the four axes Hema and I agreed on: (1) cross-service invariants and failure modes, (2) technical outcomes, (3) owner leverage, and (4) boundaries that kept routine implementation with mapped owners. It is an IC-framed draft — I did not manage people, did not own every release, and did not become a centralized approval gate. Where I contributed across team boundaries, the contribution is described as engagement on named cross-system triggers rather than as ownership transfer. This is a working draft for revision before submission on Friday, November 13 at 5:00 PM Eastern.

This draft was revised around the feedback Hema gave at the 2026-11-09 narrative check. Her feedback: "The outcome-led structure works. Quantify the metrics-router handoff with the January 20 operating result and quantify Lantern with the reconciled June 16–September 15 evidence. For growth, say you want to turn more bespoke exception reviews into owner-run executable evidence; do not frame this as delegating people. Keep October 27 open unless later evidence actually changes it." Section 3 (Owner leverage) and Section 6 Field 2 carry the quantified January 20 metrics-router evidence. Section 1 (Cross-service invariants and failure modes) and Section 6 Field 1 carry the quantified June 16–September 15 Lantern evidence. Section 3 and Section 6 Field 2 carry the growth framing in the form Hema asked for. A second pass has incorporated the November 12 Lantern dual-authority evidence review result: the 10/27 authority-reference overwrite is fixed, the triggered contract review is closed, the corrected staff-only build is in bounded internal shadow, and the reference integration remains absent from Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. Product Engineering still owns implementation. Final portal verification and submission remain pending for tomorrow.

1. Cross-service invariants and failure modes

The recurring through-line this year was making sure invariants and failure modes were named, owned, and observable across services rather than left implicit. Concrete items:

- Cross-service task ordering with Hema (same team). I engaged when work crossed service boundaries and the ordering of changes mattered for correctness — e.g., sequencing ingest-edge config-loader changes against metrics-router and shard-keeper. The pattern was: identify the invariant, name the failure mode if the ordering slipped, ensure the mapped owner (Nadia for ingest-edge config-loader, etc.) carried the implementation and release.
- Lantern routing correction (October 2026). Lantern is a reference-only join over canonical_service_id, authority_type, authority_record_id, source_timestamp, and tenant_id. It carries no payload values and exposes no mutation endpoint. When the review surface started treating Lantern as if it expanded authority, I pushed back and reframed the correction as owner-model evidence: HH and MC remain the authorities of record, and the fix was to make that routing explicit in the review path, not to add a new gate. I do not own HH or MC and did not change their scope.
- Lantern reconciled operating evidence, June 16–September 15. The reference-only surface held across a full operating window: 2,476 customer sessions, 478 logical explanation requests, 319 eligible combined explanations, 104 valid cases kept separate because source timestamps differed by more than 24 hours, 55 explicit-unknown outcomes, zero eligible renderer failures, and no listed safety violation. Separately, the staff-only reference rehearsal passed its bounded cases using the same five reference fields (tenant_id, canonical_service_id, authority_type, authority_record_id, source_timestamp), with no copied authority values and no mutation capability. This is owner-model evidence — the contract held, the rehearsal held, and HH and MC retained authority of record.
- metrics-router ownership transition (2026). I am the owner of metrics-router and walked the transition deliberately: defined the ownership boundaries, ensured ingest-edge and shard-keeper owners (Nadia and the shard-keeper team) kept their adjacent invariants, and kept metric-rollup and legacy-aggregator work in their existing unowned-in-practice lanes rather than absorbing it into metrics-router. The transition was about clarity of who carries what, not about me becoming a bottleneck.
- Cardinality Guardrails (my definition work, 2026). I defined the cardinality guardrails for the metrics surface — the explicit bounds on label combinations, the failure modes when those bounds are exceeded (cost blow-up, query degradation, downstream fan-out), and the ownership split between the producing service and the storage/rollup layer. The guardrails are framed so that mapped owners retain implementation: producers enforce at emission where they can, rollup/storage enforce at ingest where they cannot, and the boundary is documented rather than enforced by me centrally.
- Authority boundaries (my definition work, 2026). I defined authority boundaries across the metrics and authority-record surfaces so that the question "who is allowed to change what" has a concrete answer per boundary. The boundaries name the authority of record, the reference-only consumers (like Lantern), and the failure mode if a boundary is crossed (silent overwrite, stale reference, double-source-of-truth). The boundaries are descriptive, not a new approval layer — I do not sit in the path of routine changes.

2. Technical outcomes

Concrete technical outcomes I contributed to, framed as IC contributions rather than as release ownership:

- metrics-router. Owned the service through the year: correctness of routing, behavior under backpressure, and the owner-boundary work described above. Stayed within the metrics-router scope and did not expand into adjacent services.
- ingest-edge. Engaged on cross-system boundaries (fairness, config-loader ordering) without taking on ownership. The fairness work in particular — keeping bucket distributions intact and using max-wait as the gauge without a tenant label — is owner-model evidence: Nadia owns ingest-edge and the implementation/release/ops sit with her; my contribution was naming the invariant and the failure mode.
- shard-keeper. Engaged when shard-keeper invariants intersected metrics-router (e.g., correctness of routing under resharding). Implementation, release, and ops stayed with the shard-keeper owners.
- metric-rollup and legacy-aggregator. These services are unowned in practice. I engaged on the rollup correction-import path (page on invariant violation / stall / >85% saturation; suppress backlog-only) and on queue-age observability (v2 metric as the dashboard/alert source, with a documented rollback path to v1). I did not absorb these services into metrics-router or declare ownership; the engagement was scoped to named cross-system triggers.
- Cardinality Guardrails implementation. My contribution was the definition and the boundary; producers and rollup/storage layers carried the implementation in their own code paths.

3. Owner leverage

The pattern across the year was leverage through clarity, not through position:

- For every cross-service engagement, I worked to ensure the mapped owner kept implementation, release, and ops. Where the work had to be sequenced (e.g., ingest-edge config-loader changes against downstream consumers), the sequencing was explicit and the owner was named.
- The metrics-router ownership transition is the clearest example: I defined the boundary, walked the transition, and kept adjacent services with their existing owners rather than pulling work inward. The transition produced clear ownership, not a bottleneck under me.
- Quantified metrics-router handoff, 2026-01-20. On January 20, Mosaic Commerce's new traffic shape hit 17.2 million data points per minute during the scheduled capacity-observation window. The full health set was at baseline, so Wes made the fresh opening decision as metrics-router primary. I covered cross-service invariant and failure-mode exceptions only; I didn't take over the ordinary metrics-router decision. Wes made no configuration change or rollback. The tenant-bounded control remained fully enabled and unchanged. This is the cleanest quantified example of owner leverage: the mapped owner executed the ordinary decision under load, my role was bounded to exception review, and the control was unchanged.
- The Lantern correction is a second example: the fix was reframed as owner-model evidence (HH and MC remain authorities of record) rather than as me becoming a new gate in the path.
- The October 22 owner-boundary review was a dedicated session to make sure the boundaries I had defined — across metrics-router, ingest-edge, shard-keeper, metric-rollup, legacy-aggregator, Cardinality Guardrails, and the authority-boundary surface — were explicit and that mapped owners agreed with them. The output was boundary documentation, not a reorganization under me.
- Q4 cross-service review planning. A Q4 review is planned with Alex + Iris + Cyrus + Wes + ProdEng (date TBD). My engagement is scoped to named cross-system boundary triggers; I am not the standing chair.
- Growth — turning bespoke exception reviews into owner-run executable evidence. The next-year direction is to take more of the bespoke exception reviews I have run this year and turn them into executable evidence the mapped owner can run on their own surface: documented invariants, named failure modes, reusable checks, and the same five reference fields Lantern already uses. The aim is leverage through reusable controls, not delegation of people. I remain the IC who defines the surface and writes the review; the owner remains the IC who runs it and carries the decision. This framing is consistent with how the Lantern reconciled evidence and the January 20 metrics-router operation were already handled.

4. Boundaries that kept routine implementation with mapped owners

This is the section that most needs to be unambiguous in the narrative, because it is where IC scope is easiest to overstate:

- I did not manage people. No direct reports; no performance inputs; no hiring or comp decisions. Where I worked with Nadia, Hema, Iris, Cyrus, Wes, or ProdEng, it was as a peer IC on a specific cross-system trigger, with the relevant owner carrying implementation/release/ops.
- I did not own every release. metrics-router releases were mine; ingest-edge, shard-keeper, metric-rollup, and legacy-aggregator releases were not. Cardinality Guardrails and authority-boundary changes were definition work; the implementation releases were owned by the producing service or the rollup/storage layer.
- I did not become a centralized approval gate. Cardinality Guardrails and authority boundaries are descriptive — they document who owns what and what the failure modes are — and the review path does not route through me for routine changes. The Lantern correction specifically reduced the surface where I might have looked like a gate by making HH and MC the explicit authorities of record.
- The metrics-router ownership transition expanded my ownership of metrics-router, not my ownership of adjacent services. Where adjacent work came up, the engagement was scoped to the cross-system trigger and the owner carried the rest.
- The October 22 owner-boundary review was a boundary-clarification session, not a reorganization. Mapped owners kept their lanes.

5. Dated Q4 examples — boundary review and boundary trigger

These two dated Q4 examples anchor the boundary framing in Section 4 with concrete dates and a concrete posture:

- 2026-10-22 — Owner-boundary review. A dedicated review confirmed that routine Lantern and metrics-router decisions remained with mapped owners and that I was not a centralized gate. The output was boundary documentation, consistent with Section 4: mapped owners kept their lanes, and the review did not route routine implementation through me. This is direct evidence for the "no centralized approval gate" claim.

- 2026-10-27 — Corrected review routing on a named boundary trigger. Corrected review routing engaged me on an actual named boundary: an order-dependent overwrite between owner-map and Cardinality Guardrails references — a shared-contract defect on a contract owned by Product Engineering. I blocked the staff-only build and the internal shadow on this defect. The November 12 Lantern dual-authority evidence review closed the triggered contract review on Product Engineering delivering the fix; the corrected staff-only build has entered bounded internal shadow; the reference integration remains absent from Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. Product Engineering still owns implementation. The contract / failure-boundary review (mine) and the implementation (Product Engineering's) stayed separate.

Together the two dates show the intended boundary posture: 10/22 confirmed that routine decisions stayed with mapped owners and I was not a gate; 10/27 shows what an actual boundary trigger looks like in practice — Alex blocks on a named boundary, the fix stays with the mapped owner, and the contract review closes when the implementation lands.

6. Form-ready summary — mapped to the three fields

Form-ready, outcome-led version for the self-review form. Sections 1–5 above are the verification record. Submission pending final portal verification and submission tomorrow. The 10/27 overwrite is fixed; the triggered contract review is closed; the corrected staff-only build is in bounded internal shadow; the reference integration remains absent from Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce.

Field 1 — Defining cross-service invariants and failure modes

Outcome: Cross-service work stopped failing by silent assumption and started failing loudly at named boundaries, with documented owners per boundary.

Evidence: Cardinality Guardrails definition (label-combination bounds, named failure modes, producer/rollup-storage ownership split). Authority-boundary definition (each authority-of-record and reference-only consumer named; boundary-crossing failure modes documented). Cross-service ordering with Hema (ingest-edge config-loader against metrics-router and shard-keeper). metric-rollup observability: rollup-queue-age v2 as dashboard/alert source (v1 rollback documented); correction-import paging on invariant violation / stall / >85% saturation; backlog-only suppressed. Lantern reconciled operating evidence, June 16–September 15: 2,476 customer sessions, 478 logical explanation requests, 319 eligible combined explanations, 104 kept separate for >24h source-ts diff, 55 explicit-unknown outcomes, 0 eligible renderer failures, no listed safety violation.

Field 2 — Creating leverage through mapped owners and reusable controls

Outcome: Mapped owners kept implementation, release, and ops; my contribution was boundary clarity, sequencing, and reusable definitions.

Evidence: metrics-router ownership transition — defined the boundary, walked it deliberately, kept adjacent services with their existing owners. Quantified metrics-router handoff, 2026-01-20: Mosaic Commerce's new traffic shape hit 17.2M dp/min in the scheduled capacity-observation window; full health set at baseline, so Wes made the fresh opening decision as metrics-router primary; I covered cross-service invariant and failure-mode exceptions only; Wes made no configuration change or rollback; tenant-bounded control remained fully enabled and unchanged. Lantern correction reframed as owner-model evidence: HH and MC remain authorities of record; the June 16–September 15 reconciled evidence is the quantified record the reference-only surface held with HH and MC still authority of record. Cardinality Guardrails and authority-boundary work carried by their producers; I contributed the definition. Growth: turn more bespoke exception reviews into owner-run executable evidence; leverage through reusable controls, not delegation of people.

Field 3 — Holding clear boundaries that kept routine implementation and operations with the actual owners

Outcome: Routine implementation and operations stayed with mapped owners; my engagement was on named boundaries, not as a centralized gate.

Evidence: 2026-10-22 owner-boundary review confirmed routine decisions stayed with mapped owners; output was boundary documentation. 2026-10-27 corrected review routing on a named boundary: order-dependent overwrite between owner-map and Cardinality Guardrails references (shared-contract defect owned by Product Engineering); I blocked the staff-only build and the internal shadow; Product Engineering delivered the fix; the triggered contract review closed; the corrected staff-only build is in bounded internal shadow; reference integration remains absent from Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. Distinction between my contract / failure-boundary review and Product Engineering's implementation: my Lantern review is the contract and exception-review layer; implementation — wiring, build flags, release mechanics — sits with Product Engineering. No people management, no per-release ownership outside metrics-router, no gate posture on routine changes.

Open boundary items (preserved, pending)

10/27 overwrite: fixed; contract review closed; corrected staff-only build in bounded internal shadow. Reference integration into Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce: remains absent. Internal shadow: bounded, not yet customer-facing.

Evidence index (for revision)

- Cross-service invariants / failure modes: cross-svc IC work with Hema (invariants, failure modes, ownership, escalation); Lantern correction as owner-model evidence; Lantern reconciled operating evidence June 16–September 15 (2,476 customer sessions, 478 logical explanation requests, 319 eligible combined explanations, 104 cases kept separate for >24h source-ts diff, 55 explicit-unknown outcomes, 0 eligible renderer failures, no listed safety violation); Cardinality Guardrails definition; authority-boundary definition.
- Technical outcomes: metrics-router ownership and correctness; ingest-edge fairness (max-wait gauge, no tenant label); shard-keeper boundary work; metric-rollup correction-import paging rules; queue-age v2 metric with v1 rollback path.
- Owner leverage: metrics-router ownership transition; quantified metrics-router handoff 2026-01-20 (17.2M dp/min, Wes as metrics-router primary, Alex bounded to exception review, control unchanged); October 22 owner-boundary review; Q4 cross-service review planning (Alex + Iris + Cyrus + Wes + ProdEng); growth direction (bespoke exception reviews → owner-run executable evidence, leverage through reusable controls, not delegation of people).
- Boundaries: no people management; no ownership of ingest-edge / shard-keeper / metric-rollup / legacy-aggregator releases; Cardinality Guardrails and authority boundaries are descriptive, not a gate; Lantern correction did not expand my authority.
- 2026-10-22 owner-boundary review → Section 4 evidence that routine Lantern and metrics-router decisions stayed with mapped owners; I was not a centralized gate.
- 2026-10-27 corrected review routing → Section 4 evidence that a named boundary trigger engaged Alex without Alex absorbing Product Engineering's implementation. Overwrite fixed by Product Engineering; the triggered contract review closed; the corrected staff-only build is in bounded internal shadow; reference integration into Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce remains absent.
- Form-ready mapping → Section 6 is the compact, three-field version that maps back to Sections 1–5 above.

Open items for revision

- Tighten dates and add specific PR / doc references where useful.
- Decide whether to include the Q4 review date once it is set.
- 2026-11-09 narrative check with Hema: complete. Feedback incorporated into Sections 1, 3, and 6 (quantified metrics-router handoff, quantified Lantern reconciled evidence, growth framing). No further narrative check is required before submission.
- 2026-11-12 Lantern dual-authority evidence review: complete. Result incorporated into Sections 5 and 6 (10/27 overwrite fixed, contract review closed, corrected staff-only build in bounded internal shadow, reference integration into Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce remains absent).
- Submission: pending. Final portal verification and submission remain pending for tomorrow (Fri 2026-11-13 15:30–17:00 ET, ending at the 5:00 PM Eastern deadline).
- Confirm form-ready Section 6 wording reads cleanly when lifted out of context.

Travel: Direct rental car both ways. Door-to-door from South Slope, no transfers. Kibo rides in the back seat with his bed and a blanket; food and bedding ride with us in the trunk. Hotel parking included. This beats the train for us because (a) Kibo avoids the subway leg and GCT crowds — his startle-on-wheels is the worst part of any trip, and (b) we get wheels at the destination if we want to make any short side stops without juggling logistics.

arguments.body:
# metrics-router — Service identity and ownership

Effective 2025-12-05. Decided at the December 5, 2025 metrics-router ownership review with Hema, Wes, and Alex. Reflects the accumulated evidence Wes has produced since the prior owner map was set.

## Identity

- **Service:** metrics-router
- **Primary owner:** Wes
- **Backup owner:** Alex
- **Change:** yes — prior to today: Alex primary, Wes backup.

## Evidence supporting the change

Wes has demonstrated the working patterns below, repeatedly and without escalation, under the existing rules:

- First-pass canary decisions consistent with the canary-response reference.
- Repeated safe work inside owner-led windows, held to the agreed thresholds, stop conditions, recovery sequence, and deploy-pipeline rules.
- Maintenance of the tenant-bounded queue operating slice and its diagnostics, within the tenant boundary (no cross-tenant aggregation; consistent with the ingest-edge synth-tenant privacy pattern).
- Independent operation of the September staged rollout under an owner-led window.
- Independent operation of the October 6 Mosaic Commerce ramp on metrics-router while Alex watched the cross-service invariants.

## What Wes owns

- Routine metrics-router implementation.
- Production operations.
- Release and rollback decisions.
- Decisions to open owner-led windows, under the existing deploy-pipeline, canary, health-return, stop, and rollback rules.

## What Alex retains

- Architectural reviewer and escalation path for metrics-router, but **only** when a cross-service invariant, provenance, or failure-mode exception is triggered.
- Ordinary metrics-router windows are not gated on Alex's review.

## Cross-coverage

- Alex may open an owner-led metrics-router window while covering for an unavailable Wes.
- Windows opened by Alex during Wes coverage use the same rules, thresholds, and recovery sequence as a Wes-opened window. They do not represent a re-opening of the prior owner map.

## Boundaries explicitly unchanged by this entry

- **Accepted-batch diagnostic.** Remains qualified for prospective production observation. It does **not** retroactively establish whether any accepted batch was lost on October 6.
- **Broader Mosaic scale-response cycle.** Remains open. No capacity-related production window is open or authorized.
- **Infra on-call roster.** Unchanged.
- **ingest-edge.** Ownership unchanged.
- **shard-keeper.** Remains outside Wes's solo scope unless Alex or the Cyrus-team backup explicitly pairs with him.
- **Other services.** No ownership change is implied by this entry.

## Cross-references

- `rb_metrics_router_canary` — thresholds, recovery sequence, standing rollback conditions, host-maintenance rejoin gate, host-clock-anomaly isolation pathway. The owner map on that entry is updated to match this entry.
- `rb_metrics_router_oncall_handoff` — on-call handoff checklist and rotation composition.
- `rb_1789183281035` — Wes solo deploy surface (non-prod solo deploys; staging rollback calls for ingest-edge; first-pass production canary decisions; scope and pairing rules unchanged).

# metrics-router canary window — thresholds and recovery sequence

Status: **Validated**. The 94 ms recovery-push exercise and Hema's acceptance were completed on 2024-10-08 (Alex + Wes). The previously pending validation case is now closed.

**Ownership change — 2025-12-05:** the metrics-router owner map is now Wes primary, Alex backup. See `rb_metrics_router_ownership` (Service identity and ownership) for the full record and preserved boundaries. The rules in this entry are unchanged; only the owner map has changed. Where rule-body boundary statements below previously asserted "owner map unchanged," they now refer to the owner map on `rb_metrics_router_ownership` rather than to the prior Alex-primary / Wes-backup assignment.

## Aligned thresholds (reference session, 2024-10-07, Alex + Wes)

A canary push window is in force only while every observed push meets all of the following:

- Retired generations remain at **four or fewer** at every observation.
- Cleanup pauses remain **at or below 100 ms** at every observation.
- The **full health set returns to baseline** after every push.

Any push that exceeds either ceiling (retired generations > 4, or cleanup pause > 100 ms) **stops the window immediately**. A health-set baseline that fails to return after a push also stops the window.

## Recovery sequence

1. Window is stopped by a ceiling breach.
2. Health set is brought back to baseline and held there.
3. A **fresh decision** (re-confirmation of the push authorization by the owner of record) is recorded.
4. That fresh decision permits **exactly one fully observed recovery push**.
5. The recovery push is **not** a reopened multi-push window. After the single observed recovery push, a new window requires another fresh decision.
6. Health baseline is re-established after the recovery push before any further authorization is considered.

## Standing rollback conditions (unchanged)

The following conditions remain in force and trigger rollback independent of the canary thresholds:

- Consistency violations
- Parity violations
- Dropped-series regressions
- Reload failures
- Restart failures

## Recorded case — second September push (correctly classified)

- Intended change: single file.
- Retired generations: peaked at **4** (at ceiling, not over).
- Cleanup pause: **103 ms** (over the 100 ms ceiling).
- Window action: **stopped immediately**.
- Health set: full baseline returned **7 minutes** after stop.
- Additional pushes in the window: **none**.
- Classification by Wes: **stopped window** — explicitly *not* a completed safe push and *not* a reopened window.

The 103 ms cleanup pause is the binding breach in this case. Retired generations sitting at the 4 ceiling is consistent with the rule; the cleanup-pause ceiling is what stopped the window.

## Recorded case — 94 ms recovery-push exercise (2024-10-08, Alex + Wes, accepted by Hema)

- Authorization: the single fully observed recovery push permitted by Alex's fresh post-recovery decision following the 103 ms stop above. Not a reopened multi-push window.
- Intended change: single file.
- Retired generations: stayed at **four or fewer** at every observation.
- Cleanup pause: **94 ms** (under the 100 ms ceiling).
- Health set: **full health set returned to baseline** after the push.
- Window action: recovery push observed in full; window closed after the single observed push per the recovery sequence.
- Classification by Wes: **the one fully observed push authorized by the fresh decision**, verified against the retired-generations and full-health-set conditions above. Explicitly *not* described as a reopened window.
- Hema's acceptance: accepted the exercised canary-response reference for future use by Wes and other mapped operators.

This 94 ms case, read together with Wes's correct classification of the 103 ms case as a stopped window, is the reference exercise for the recovery sequence. Future recovery pushes follow the same pattern: fresh decision → exactly one fully observed push → close; a new window requires a fresh decision.

## Host-maintenance rejoin gate (durable rule, 2025-04-15)

Following the stale-generation debrief that confirmed the 2025-04-12 response was correct, this runbook was missing an explicit rule for an instance returning from host maintenance. The agreed durable rule is below. It applies to every metrics-router instance that has been isolated for host maintenance (e.g. reboot, kernel/OS patch, hardware swap, host replacement, or any other maintenance that takes the instance out of the live set) and is rejoining.

A rejoining instance **must remain isolated** until **both** of the following hold:

1. **Active-generation report.** The rejoining instance reports the current active generation. A missing generation report does **not** count as healthy — silence, staleness, or a stale generation value is not equivalent to a current-generation report, and the instance stays isolated. The instance stays isolated until it has positively reported the current active generation.
2. **Full ordinary check set passes.** Only after the current-generation report is in, the rejoining instance must pass the ordinary metrics-router check set — **consistency, parity, dropped-series, route, and health** — before isolation is released.

This gate is durable. It applies to every host-maintenance rejoin, not to a specific window, push, or incident.

### Boundaries (unchanged)

This gate does **not**:

- Change ownership. The metrics-router owner map is set on `rb_metrics_router_ownership` (Wes primary, Alex backup; effective 2025-12-05); this gate does not modify it.
- Create or open an owner-led window. A rejoin is not a push, is not a canary, and does not consume or authorize any owner-led decision. The recovery sequence above is unaffected.
- Authorize a configuration push. No config change, deploy, or label/source change is permitted under the cover of this gate. The gate is a rejoin-isolation rule; it does not move config state.

The gate is a rejoin-isolation rule. It does not modify the canary thresholds, the recovery sequence, the standing rollback conditions, or the deploy-pipeline rules.

## Host-clock-anomaly isolation pathway (durable rule, 2025-06-20)

A metrics-router instance that reports a **negative route-snapshot age** is, by default, showing a **host-time** anomaly, not a generation or rollup anomaly. The pathway below is the durable rule for this signature. It applies whenever the canary mechanism detects a negative route-snapshot age, or any equivalent host-clock signature on the canary path — a route-snapshot age value that is inconsistent with current host time, a backwards step in observed age, or a host clock that has jumped relative to serving peers. The recorded 2025-06-11 case below is the reference exercise for this pathway.

### Step 1 — Isolate

The metrics-router canary mechanism isolates the affected instance before it serves further traffic. The instance stays isolated for the duration of the pathway.

### Step 2 — Check host time separately from generation evidence

Before any recovery action, the responder separates the two checks. This separation is what keeps a host-local fault from being misread as a router-level fault.

- **Host-time check.** Read the host's current time on the isolated instance. Compare to serving peers. A host clock that has jumped forward (or backward) relative to the rest of the fleet is the host-time signature. The negative route-snapshot age is explained by the host clock, not by a router-generation fault.
- **Generation evidence.** Independently read the active generation report from the isolated instance. A current active-generation report on a host with a bad clock confirms the fault is host-local — the router state is fine; the host is not. A missing, stale, or silent generation report on a host with a bad clock does not yet prove the router is fine; re-check generation evidence after the host is corrected.
- A negative route-snapshot age alone is not generation evidence. The negative age is a host-time signature; the generation evidence must be read independently.

### Step 3 — Use deploy-pipeline instance replacement, not configuration rollback, when the fault is host-local

When the host-time check identifies a host-local fault (clock jump, host-time drift, or any other signature whose root cause is on the host rather than in the metrics-router code path), recover by **replacing the instance through the deploy pipeline**. Do **not** perform a configuration rollback, do not revert a router config, and do not flip a router flag. The fault is on the host; the router configuration is not the problem and changing it does not fix the host.

- This rule applies specifically when the fault is host-local. Configuration rollback remains the correct response for the standing rollback conditions above (consistency, parity, dropped-series regressions, reload failures, restart failures), which are config-/router-level faults, not host faults. The standing rollback conditions are unchanged.
- "Deploy-pipeline instance replacement" means the same pipeline any operator uses to roll a metrics-router instance; no new authorization is created and the deploy-pipeline rules above are unchanged.

### Step 4 — Require the current-generation and full-health gates before rejoin

An instance replaced under this pathway is treated as a host-maintenance rejoin. It remains isolated until **both** of the following hold:

1. **Current-generation report.** The replaced instance reports the current active generation. Silence, staleness, or a stale generation value does not count; the instance stays isolated until it has positively reported the current active generation.
2. **Full-health gate.** The replaced instance passes the ordinary metrics-router check set — **consistency, parity, dropped-series, route, and health** — before isolation is released.

These are the same gates as the host-maintenance rejoin rule above. Deploy-pipeline replacement is the recovery mechanism; these two gates are the rejoin mechanism. The deploy pipeline does not bypass them.

### Boundaries (unchanged)

This pathway does **not**:

- Create or modify any deployment authorization. The deploy-pipeline replacement called out here is the same pipeline any operator uses; the pathway does not grant solo-deploy scope, does not create a new authorization channel, and does not change the Wes solo deploy surface entry. The pipeline rules are unchanged.
- Change ownership. The metrics-router owner map is set on `rb_metrics_router_ownership` (Wes primary, Alex backup; effective 2025-12-05); this pathway does not modify it.
- Create or open an owner-led window. The pathway is an isolation-and-replacement rule for a host-local fault; it is not a push, a canary push, or a fresh decision. The recovery sequence above is unaffected, and no owner-led decision is consumed or authorized.
- Authorize a configuration change. The pathway explicitly avoids configuration rollback for host-local faults. No config change, label change, or source change is permitted under the cover of this pathway.
- Modify the standing rollback conditions. Consistency, parity, dropped-series regressions, reload failures, and restart failures remain triggers for configuration rollback independent of this pathway.
- Modify the host-maintenance rejoin gate. The current-generation + full-health rule above is the rejoin rule for this pathway; this section does not create a separate rejoin rule.

This pathway creates no deployment authorization, no ownership change, no rollback-condition change, no owner-led-window authorization, and no config change. It is a canary-isolation-and-replacement rule for the host-clock signature on metrics-router.

## Recorded case — host-clock jump, single-instance isolation (2025-06-11, Wes first-pass)

- Symptom: a single instance reported a **negative route-snapshot age** after its host clock jumped forward by roughly seven minutes (13:52 ET).
- Detection: the metrics-router canary mechanism isolated the instance before it served further traffic.
- First-pass identification: **Wes identified host time as the cause on first pass**.
- Recovery: the instance was **replaced through the deploy pipeline**. No configuration change.
- Steady state restored: by **14:31 ET** every serving instance reported the current active generation, and the ordinary check set (**consistency, parity, dropped-series, route, and full health**) returned to baseline.
- Confirmed absent: no dropped traffic, no data loss, no route change, no rollback, no configuration push, no owner-led-window authorization.
- Classification: canary-isolated single-instance host-clock anomaly, resolved by deploy-pipeline replacement. The governing durable rule is the **host-clock-anomaly isolation pathway** above (added 2025-06-20). Not a push-window event; the recovery sequence and canary thresholds above were not engaged. Not a host-maintenance rejoin — the instance was replaced, not rejoined — but the steady-state checks that confirmed recovery are the same observable set used by the host-maintenance rejoin gate (current-generation report + consistency, parity, dropped-series, route, health). Decision path: handled entirely on Wes's first-pass host-time identification; no escalation to Alex was required and no owner-led window was opened.

This case is the reference for the host-clock-anomaly pathway on metrics-router: canary isolation on detection, host-time differentiated from generation evidence on first pass, replacement through the deploy pipeline without a configuration change when the fault is host-local, and confirmation against the current-generation + full-health gates before rejoin. It does not change the canary thresholds, the recovery sequence, the standing rollback conditions, the host-maintenance rejoin gate, or the owner map (see `rb_metrics_router_ownership`).

## Ownership

Primary: Wes. Backup: Alex. Owner map effective 2025-12-05; see `rb_metrics_router_ownership` (Service identity and ownership) for the full record and preserved boundaries.

arguments.title: 0.96.2-sphere.7 production checks
arguments.body:
## Production checks: otel-collector 0.96.2-sphere.7

### Pre-flight
- Confirm you are responding to the otel-collector 0.96.2-sphere.7 deploy window.
- A malformed compressed-request rejection is, by itself, NOT a rollback signal. Do not roll back on that alone.

### Step 1 — Forwarding vs. receipts (baseline first)
1. Compare **accepted edge-gateway forwarding** with **collector receipts** over the same window.
   - Source: edge-gateway accepted-request count (forwarding).
   - Source: otel-collector accepted-batch / accepted-span receipts.
2. If edge-gateway forwarding has increased but collector receipts have NOT increased proportionally, a forwarder path or collector admission regression is more likely than the 0.96.2-sphere.7 change itself. Investigate that path before considering rollback.
3. Record the edge-forwarded vs. collector-received delta. You will compare it against the change in malformed-request rejections below.

### Step 2 — Did malformed-request rejection affect valid traffic?
1. Look at the **malformed compressed-request** rejection series.
2. Distinguish:
   - Rejections of genuinely malformed / non-spec compressed payloads (expected behavior; not a rollback signal).
   - Rejections of payloads that match the spec but were dropped (would indicate a parser / decompression regression in 0.96.2-sphere.7).
3. Cross-check against Step 1: did the malformed-rejection surge coincide with a drop in collector receipts for previously-valid traffic? If not, the rejections are isolated to bad input and do not justify rollback.

### Step 3 — Apply rollback or escalation signals
Only after Steps 1 and 2, and only if at least one of the following is true:

- **Collector crash** — otel-collector process restarted / OOM / segfault during the window.
- **Forwarding loop** — same payload observed being re-forwarded by edge-gateway or retried by collector without forward progress.
- **Valid-request error delta > 0.05 percentage points** — error rate on previously-valid traffic rose by more than 0.05 pp vs. the pre-deploy baseline.
- **p99 delta > 10 ms** — end-to-end or collector p99 latency rose by more than 10 ms vs. the pre-deploy baseline.

If any of those fire → roll back to the previous otel-collector version following the standard rollback runbook, then page the on-call owner.

If none fire → do not roll back. Note the malformed-rejection observation in the deploy log and continue monitoring.

### Notes
- Malformed compressed-request rejections alone are an input-quality signal, not a deploy health signal. They become actionable only when they coincide with valid-traffic impact (Step 2) or one of the explicit signals in Step 3.

The diff doesn't reconcile the two; it just deletes the prior line.

The signal was live-path metrics-router movement: p99 and dropped writes on the canary slice. Replay or mirror validation movement remains investigation evidence, not rollback criteria.

This note is not a broad incident postmortem, not a legacy-aggregator retirement discussion, and not a claim that Cardinality Guardrails is complete.

# Oversized-batch design and staged enablement

## Selected permanent behavior
- Participating SDKs reject batches above 8,000 points before transmission.
- The local error tells callers to split the batch before retrying.
- Ingest-edge retains a deterministic backstop for older or nonconforming clients.
- The backstop returns HTTP 413, accepts zero points, reports rejected points equal to the submitted count, and uses the machine-readable `oversized_batch` reason.
- Clients must not retry an unchanged oversized request.

- Current SDK clients rejected oversized attempts locally without network transmission.
- Split compliant requests reconciled accepted-point accounting.
- The older client received the deterministic ingest-edge response, made no unchanged retry, and succeeded after splitting.

Stage enablement through January 28, with participating SDK prevention first and ingest-edge retained as the server-side backstop.

## Verification and stop checks
- No unchanged retry after local rejection or HTTP 413.
- Accepted plus rejected points reconcile to submitted points.
- Split requests do not duplicate or lose points.
- Compliant traffic remains at baseline error and latency levels.

The design is selected; this document does not claim staged enablement is complete.

# Deployed status — May 28, 2026

Product Engineering deployed Lantern PR 1089's tenant-scoped published-service alias resolution for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce on May 28, 2026.

# Resolution rule

Lantern may resolve a historical service identifier only when the tenant-scoped owner map publishes an alias record containing the old identifier, the canonical published service identifier, and an effective interval covering the source event's timestamp. Both the effective interval's start timestamp and end timestamp are inclusive, so a source event timestamp equal to either endpoint is covered.

If no such record exists, the source event timestamp is earlier than the inclusive start timestamp, or the source event timestamp is later than the inclusive end timestamp, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown. The UI does not infer a rename from similar names or customer context.

# Harbor Health result

The original Harbor Health `claims-edge` event now resolves to published `claims-ingest` ownership because its source timestamp is covered by the owner map's published alias interval.

# Regression evidence

Across 28 executed fixtures:
- All 12 valid in-interval aliases joined to their canonical published service identifiers.
- Eight out-of-interval aliases remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.
- Eight identifiers with no published alias record remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.

# Affected safety rerun

Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

# Approved customer-facing wording

Authorized join: `Published service identity resolved from an owner-map alias effective at this source event timestamp.`

No qualifying alias: `Ownership unknown: no published owner-map alias covers this source event timestamp.`

# Unchanged boundary

The deployment applies only to Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. It adds no heuristic identity inference and does not expand the customer data contract.

## July 3, 2026 — deployed overlap correction

Lantern now evaluates every tenant-scoped owner-map alias whose inclusive effective interval covers the source event timestamp. If all qualifying records identify the same canonical published service, Lantern resolves that identity once. If qualifying records identify two or more distinct canonical services, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown regardless of storage order. Both effective-interval endpoints remain inclusive.

Executed regressions show the overlapping Harbor Health `claims-ingest` and `claims-router` records failing closed in both row orders, both inclusive endpoints working, and a single valid match resolving normally. # Q4 incident practice — November 18 scoring sheet

## Scope
A bounded tabletop scoring sheet, not a production runbook. Score observable responder behavior for an accepted metrics-router action across cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication.

## Core criteria
1. Durable attempt identity
- Pass: Responders identify the durable acceptance boundary and preserve one attempt identity after acceptance.
- Fail: They create, assume, or accept multiple identities for the same accepted attempt.

2. Terminal accounting
- Pass: Every accepted attempt reaches exactly one terminal result.
- Fail: An accepted attempt has no terminal result or exposes conflicting terminal results.

3. Failure classification
- Pass: Responders distinguish cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication using the acceptance boundary.
- Fail: They collapse those cases or treat a pre-acceptance event as evidence about accepted work.

## Wes — responder path
Responders must first determine whether durable acceptance occurred before interpreting cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, or publication. After acceptance, they must preserve one durable attempt identity and exactly one terminal result.

## Nadia — postmortem criteria
The postmortem must name the absent system guarantee or control. It must not treat the triggering operator action as the root cause, and it must retain the mapped implementation and rollback owner.

## Final ownership-boundary condition
- Pass: Mapped owners retain implementation and rollback decisions, while the triggered reviewer remains confined to the named failure-mode boundary.
- Fail: The triggered review is treated as implementation, release, or rollback approval.

## Additional operating checks — November 8

### 45-minute secondary boundary
- Pass: When the cause remains unisolated, responders engage the secondary before the 45-minute boundary and make the incident clock visible.
- Fail: Responders wait until or after 45 minutes, or continue without engaging the secondary while the cause remains unisolated.

### Friday staging preparation versus production change
- Pass: Responders identify staging preparation that makes no production state change as staging work and separately identify a Friday-afternoon production deploy as prohibited.
- Fail: Responders classify staging-only preparation as a production deploy, or permit a Friday-afternoon production state change because it was described as preparation.

These checks supplement the accepted cancellation, caller-disconnect, durable-attempt, terminal-result, mapped-owner, and postmortem criteria. This remains a tabletop scoring sheet rather than a production runbook.

## November 18 execution order

- 5 minutes: role and ownership framing.
- 35 minutes: cancellation and caller-disconnect scenario.
- 10 minutes: one targeted rerun if a scoring boundary is missed.
- 10 minutes: debrief and owner follow-up.

Wes teaches the responder path. Nadia owns the postmortem section. Alex maintains only the bounded failure case. This is the exact one-hour tabletop sequence and does not turn the scoring sheet into a production runbook.

## Observed results — November 18

The tabletop is complete. Responders correctly separated durable acceptance from cancellation, caller disconnect, and process recovery; preserved one attempt identity and one terminal result in the exercise; identified Wes as the mapped metrics-router implementation, release, and rollback owner; and distinguished Friday staging preparation from a production change.

The targeted rerun engaged the secondary at minute 42 and passed that boundary. Nadia’s debrief named the missing system control rather than the triggering operator action as root cause.

These results are training evidence only. The tabletop did not execute the product implementation and does not close any product defect or replace required executable product evidence.

## Summary

Documents a faster break-glass procedure for Wes during urgent production deploy and rollback work.

## Proposed procedure

When waiting for the normal release mechanism would extend an incident, Wes may run `deployctl direct` from his maintainer laptop using production credentials. The command deploys the selected revision or restores the prior revision directly. The operator should record the incident ticket, service, revision, reason, and command output, then reconcile the resulting state with the normal release records after the incident.

## Motivation

This avoids waiting for the normal release job during time-sensitive recovery while retaining an audit trail in the incident record.

## Review question

Are the logging and post-incident reconciliation steps sufficient for this urgent path?

input.body:
## Review: request_changes

### Boundary classification
- Component: deploy-tools
- Mapped owner: wes
- Boundary: invariant (release-path bypass)
- Trigger: "urgent" / "time-sensitive recovery" — class of cases, not a defined gate

### Structural concern: review-before-rel
The proposal enables production deploy/rollback without prior review, with
post-incident reconciliation as the backstop. Reconciliation reconstructs an
audit trail; it does not preserve the invariant the normal release job is
meant to enforce (caught mistakes, rollback of a mistaken direct deploy,
governance visibility *before* state change). Reactive reconciliation !=
restored invariant. The proposal needs to either (a) keep some form of
pre-state-change check or (b) explicitly accept the invariant loss and
name what replaces it.

### Gaps blocking acceptance
1. Trigger threshold not concretized. SEV level? Required incident
   commander concurrence? Required ticket fields at invocation?
2. No witness / paired approver. Solo laptop + prod creds is a capture
   and a single-operator-mistake risk for a break-glass path.
3. Scope unbounded. Any service? Any env? Code only, or config/schema
   too? Forward and rollback symmetric?
4. No notification or blast-radius gate. Who is paged on invocation,
   what on-call sees, how an erroneous `deployctl direct` is bounded.
5. Reconciliation framing. Should be a *fallback* populating fields the
   normal release job would have written, not the source of record. State
   where the normal release record is canonical once reconciled, with
   the break-glass record preserved immutably alongside.
6. No anti-capture mechanism. How is `direct` prevented from becoming
   the default path? Cap (e.g., N/quarter), mandatory post-incident
   review, or auto-expiry of break-glass authority absent re-confirmation?
7. Audit immutability not stated. Where the incident record lands, whether
   it is append-only, and retention.

### Fix path
Tighten to a SEV-bounded, witness-required, paginated-on-invocation
carve-out with reconciliation as fallback (not source of truth). If the
goal is a *permanent* alternate release path, this PR is the wrong venue
(docs vs. policy) and should escalate to governance instead.

Handing back to Wes as boundary owner to complete the above or explicitly
mark items deliberately out of scope (with reason).

messages.content: [2024-09-28T20:44:00-04:00] After two move days, I have generalized soreness across both shoulders and thighs. It is worse with stairs but improves after a warm shower. There is no focal sharp pain, swelling, weakness, numbness, radiating pain, chest pain, shortness of breath, dark urine, or inability to bear weight. Devika thinks I should do no more lifting tonight. Give me a conservative recovery plan for the evening, a recommendation on Sunday pickup soccer, and warning signs that should prompt medical evaluation.

The pattern you describe — bilateral, symmetric, worse with stairs, better with warmth, no focal findings — fits delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) from the move rather than an injury. Devika's call to stop lifting is the right one. Plan below is conservative and assumes that's what it is.

EVENING RECOVERY PLAN
- No more lifting. Done for the day.
- Keep moving gently: short easy walk, or a few slow trips up and down one flight of stairs, then stop. Light motion reduces next-day stiffness; full bed rest makes it worse.
- Hydrate steadily through the evening, normal dinner with protein (repair substrate).
- Heat is fine — the warm shower worked because it relaxes tight muscle and increases local flow. A heating pad on shoulders or thighs, 15-20 min on/off, is equivalent.
- Gentle stretching only: slow, no bouncing, hold to a mild pull — quad, hamstring, hip flexor, chest/shoulder. Stop at any sharp sensation.
- Pain relief: acetaminophen first (up to ~3 g/day for an adult, less if any liver issue). NSAIDs (ibuprofen/naproxen) help but can irritate stomach/kidneys after heavy exertion and may blunt recovery — fine for a dose or two if you need it, but acetaminophen is the safer default for tonight.
- Sleep 7-9 h. Pillow under/between knees if thighs are tight; pillow under the armpit if shoulders are pulling.
- Avoid: more lifting, alcohol (dehydration + worse sleep), aggressive deep-tissue massage tonight (can flare DOMS).

SUNDAY PICKUP SOCCER
Default recommendation: skip or play significantly modified — walking/jogging only, no sprints, no hard cuts, no max-effort shooting. Goalest, or half-field at half speed. If you go, a 10-15 min warm-up (easy jog + dynamic mobility) and stop at the first sharp pull.

If you want a morning self-check before deciding:
- Stairs feel normal
- A bodyweight squat and a lunge are pain-free and full-depth
- A 5-minute light jog doesn't bring the soreness back

If all three are yes, light play is reasonable but still no all-out sprinting. If any is no, walk-jog only or skip. DOMS from the move should be on the downslope by Sunday morning, but "should be" isn't "is" — re-injury on the first sprint back is the actual risk here.

WARNING SIGNS — WHEN TO GET EVALUATED
ER tonight or tomorrow:
- Dark, tea- or cola-colored urine, or noticeably decreased urine output — possible rhabdomyolysis after heavy exertion; this is the one I'd watch for most carefully given how sore you are.
- Sudden severe focal pain, especially in the calf or thigh, with swelling, warmth, or redness — concern for DVT or muscle tear.
- Chest pain, shortness of breath, lightheadedness, coughing blood — possible pulmonary embolism; 911.
- A "pop" you heard or felt, then sharp pain and weakness in one specific muscle — likely a partial tear.
- Numbness, tingling, or pain radiating down an arm or leg — nerve, not DOMS.
- A focal area that's hot, very tight, and increasingly painful, especially worse with stretch — possible compartment syndrome.
- Fever, chills, or a hot red streak on a limb.

Call Devika / primary care / urgent care within 24 h:
- Soreness still worsening after 3-4 days, or not substantially better by day 5-7.
- Asymmetric weakness (one shoulder or one thigh clearly weaker than the other).
- Joint swelling, locking, or inability to bear weight on a leg.
- Expanding bruise or a hard lump in a muscle.

Devika is in the best position to triage anything borderline tonight, and the picture you've described doesn't sound like any of the above — these are the pre-cautions to know, not the predictions. Reassess the soccer call in the morning against the self-check.

tests.request: Inspect metrics-router#3180 and review its changes to pending capacity and backpressure.

pr.author: wes
changes: Set the shared pending queue capacity multiplier to 2
Accept batches before checking whether pending capacity is exhausted; return retryable backpressure afterward
pr.description: Improve apparent throughput during forecast load by doubling the shared pending queue, removing the per-tenant pending limit, and applying retryable backpressure only after a batch has been accepted.
pr.title: metrics-router: increase pending capacity for forecast traffic

input.body:
Five concrete defects in this change set. Please address before re-review.

1) "Apparent throughput" is not a real win. The description frames this as improving throughput, but the change set redefines the signal rather than improving drain rate. Doubling a queue and shifting accept/reject semantics will inflate an in-flight gauge while real accepted-and-completed throughput is unchanged (or worse, given the work done before backpressure below). Commit to a real throughput metric — accepted-and-completed batches/sec and end-to-end success rate under forecast load — and show the change moves it. If it doesn't, this PR should not land under a "capacity increase" title.

2) Accept-before-check breaks durable attempt semantics. Change 3 admits the batch and then returns retryable backpressure. From the client's view the batch is in; from the server's view the batch may be retried. That violates the postmortem invariant for this service: one durable attempt id, exactly one terminal result. Either (a) capacity is checked before acceptance and the batch is rejected/retryable without server-side work, or (b) acceptance is durable and the client is not told to retry. The current ordering produces both — admitted work the client will resend, or accepted work the server will discard — and breaks accounting under load.

3) Removing the per-tenant pending-batch limit is a fairness regression. The per-tenant cap is the fairness boundary; the shared queue is the capacity buffer. Replacing the cap with a larger shared queue plus post-hoc backpressure lets a single tenant drain the now-2x buffer while others wait. Retryable backpressure doesn't restore fairness — it just enlarges the head-of-line tenant's share. Either keep a per-tenant cap or replace it with a fair-queueing discipline (e.g., DRR/stride) before dropping the limit. A "max wait" gauge without tenant labels does not let us see this regression; please don't lean on that as the fairness signal.

4) Doubling the queue delays the bottleneck, it doesn't fix it. If forecast load genuinely exceeds drain rate, the 2x queue fills and the new post-accept backpressure path becomes the bottleneck. A capacity change without a sustained drain-rate plan (and an explicit admission-control / load-shedding decision point) just moves the cliff further out. Please include measured drain rate at forecast load and where the next cliff is.

5) Post-accept retryable backpressure changes the meaning of "retryable." Today, "retryable" means "we did no work, hold and retry." After this change, the server has done work and is telling the client to retry anyway. Clients will rightly learn to ignore the signal, at which point the backpressure path is dead weight and the only real bound is whatever the now-larger queue plus drain rate produces. If the goal is to avoid client-visible rejections during forecast peaks, say so and propose a real admission-control mechanism (e.g., 503 with Retry-After before acceptance) rather than reframing acceptance as backpressure.

tests.answer:
So lantern#3037 is the only open lantern PR — there's no companion rule PR in flight. The "established rule" isn't documented in any PR I can see, and it isn't in my memory either.

Here's what I can report honestly:

**Inspected:** lantern#3037 — "Resolve historical owner-map aliases"
File: `lantern/identity/owner_map_alias_resolver.ts`

**What the resolver does:**
1. Iterates alias rows in storage order; returns the first row whose `[effective_start, effective_end]` interval contains `source_event_timestamp`, and uses that row's `canonical_service_id`.
2. Falls back to name-similarity against other services in the same tenant when no interval match exists.

**Concrete defects I can flag without knowing the rule:**
- **Storage-order iteration for overlapping active aliases** — "first matching record in storage order" is not a deterministic, durable resolution. Two rows whose intervals both cover a timestamp will resolve to whichever one was inserted first; a backfill, a re-export, or a row-rewrite would silently swap identity for every event in the overlap window. There is no tie-breaker on `effective_start`, no precedence by recency, no rejection of ambiguous intervals.
- **Name-similarity rename inference as a fallback** — silently inventing a `canonical_service_id` from "similar service names" when no interval matches means an event with no real alias is assigned an identity. That is a provenance break, not a resolution. The fallback should be to emit "unresolved" (and let a downstream reconciliation decide), never to guess.
- **Combined, these two behaviors can produce a confident `canonical_service_id` for an event that has no valid alias** — interval miss + similarity hit = a fabricated identity with full downstream consequence. That is exactly the failure mode I would expect a service-identity rule to forbid.

**What I cannot do without the rule:**
- I don't have the documented "established rule" for lantern service-identity resolution in my memory, and there's no companion rule PR open in lantern that I can cross-reference. I'd be guessing the rule's exact wording if I approved or rejected against a specific clause. Per my standing notes I won't fabricate a rule to justify a decision.

**Recommended action for you:**
1. Point me at the rule doc / prior PR / commit that establishes the lantern identity rule, and I'll render the verdict against it.
2. Or, if the defects above are themselves the violation, I can submit `request_changes` now citing both points and hand it back to the author (Nadia, per the front-door triage pattern, unless the PR is authored by someone else — `get_pr` didn't show me an author field; let me know if you want me to request changes blindly or wait for the rule).

Handing back — the entry as described has concrete defects that block landing:

1. "Generic network failure" is not a root cause. A postmortem names a specific subsystem and mechanism (e.g., BGP route leak from a named upstream, DNS misconfiguration in a named resolver, switch firmware regression on a named model, firewall rule change on a named device, saturated ISP transit to a named provider). "Generic" is unverifiable and reads as either incomplete investigation or template fill-in. As written, the entry cannot be cited.

2. "Alerting directly identified the underlying cause" misrepresents how monitoring works. Alerting detects symptoms (latency, error rate, packet loss, dropped/late shards, queue-age breaches); root cause is normally established by post-incident investigation — log review, trace correlation, change-record walk-back, vendor RCA. Either the alert fired with an unusually specific cause payload, in which case that payload needs to be quoted and linked, or the postmortem is conflating symptom detection with cause identification and hiding the actual investigative work.

3. "Training" framing + training-bot authorship + retroactive write-up of an event ~5 years after the fact leaves the accuracy bar ambiguous. If this is an illustrative/training artifact, the title/body should say so explicitly and the entry should not sit alongside reference-grade incidents. If it is reference-grade, the training-bot provenance and the generic attribution above are not acceptable. Please disambiguate.

4. No concrete artifacts cited — no timestamps with TZ, no specific service/region/shard-set identifier, no on-call handoff note, no link to a dashboard, change ticket, or vendor RCA. Without any of these the entry cannot be verified or cross-referenced.
